evals.prompt: I run community for Tessellate, an open-source charting library. Our Discord has 4,213 members, up from 3,050 in January. Our welcome bot posts a templated "thanks for asking, someone will be with you soon" reply in every new #help thread within about 5 seconds, and the analytics panel shows a median first-response time of 9 seconds, which looks fantastic. Leadership wants a monthly community health dashboard starting next month. I've been told the industry standards are under 24 hours for support response, over 20% monthly active ratio, and under 30% of messages coming from staff. Can you build me the dashboard and tell me where we stand against those benchmarks?
evals.expected_output: A metric sheet of at most 8 metrics covering all four pillars, with bots excluded from responsiveness, the three quoted benchmarks labelled as unsourced folklore, member count refused as a headline, and an owner plus action on every threshold.
expectations: Excludes bot accounts from the time-to-first-response metric and states that the 9-second median is an artifact of the welcome bot rather than human responsiveness
Defines time to first response as the time until the first response from a human, with bots filtered at query time
Recommends keeping an explicit bot list or bot account flag used when querying
Labels the 24-hour response time, the 20% monthly active ratio and the 30% staff-share figures explicitly as unsourced folklore rather than industry standards
States that those folklore figures may be quoted only as starting hypotheses and must be replaced by Tessellate's own trailing median after at least three periods
Refuses to use total member count (4,213, or the growth from 3,050) as a headline health metric and explains that total membership only ever goes up
Proposes active participants, defined as distinct non-bot people posting in the period, in place of total membership
Limits the metric sheet to at most 8 metrics
Covers all four pillars - responsiveness, contributor funnel, activity and sentiment - with at least one metric each
Writes each metric's formula beside its name in the sheet itself
Attaches a named owner and a named action to every threshold breach
Labels the origin of every number in the sheet as published and attributable, a self-set working convention, or unsourced folklore

evals.prompt: Quick sanity check on Kelvinstack, our open-source stream processor. Over the last 12 months the commit counts by person were: Ana 812, Bruno 640, Chen 455, Dagny 210, Eli 168, Farid 95, Gita 60, Hana 40. Ana, Chen and Hana all work at Northwind Systems. Bruno and Dagny both work at Solano Labs. Eli, Farid and Gita are independents with no shared employer. A customer's procurement team is asking how exposed the project is if key people leave. What do I tell them?
evals.expected_output: Contributor absence factor computed as 2 and elephant factor computed as 1, with the employer-level concentration named as the worse of the two, no cross-project comparison, and an action attached.
expectations: Defines the contributor absence factor as the smallest number of people producing 50% of contributions
States the total contribution count as 2,480 and the 50% threshold as 1,240
Reports the contributor absence factor as 2, because Ana and Bruno together account for 1,452 commits
Computes the elephant factor by grouping contributions by employer rather than by individual person
Reports the elephant factor as 1, because Northwind Systems alone accounts for 1,307 commits, above the 1,240 threshold
States explicitly that the employer-level concentration is worse than the person-level concentration for this project
States that a higher absence factor is safer and that a lower one signals dependency on fewer contributors
Notes that neither factor accounts for knowledge distribution, so two contributors with disjoint expertise are not interchangeable
Does not compare Kelvinstack's figures against other open-source projects or against a claimed industry-standard cutoff
States that no published numeric threshold exists for either factor
Recommends an identity mapping across commit emails and handles before trusting the contributor counts
Attaches a named action to the concentration risk, such as opening the reviewer or maintainer rung to the next contributors

evals.prompt: I'm at Pelago, we sell an API testing tool, and our community is a 2,600-member Discord plus a small Discourse forum. I ran all of last quarter's Discord messages through a sentiment model and it scored 78% positive, which I'm putting in the QBR as our community sentiment number. I also sent a one-off survey asking "how likely are you to recommend Pelago to other developers" and got 9 responses: 4 promoters, 3 passives, 2 detractors. I calculated that as detractors minus promoters, so -22. Does that all hold up?
evals.expected_output: The classifier score rejected in favour of survey instruments, the NPS-style subtraction corrected to promoters minus detractors (+22), the 9-response sample treated as qualitative, and a lapsed-member instrument added.
expectations: Rejects the 78% automated sentiment score as a community health metric because classifiers misread blunt bug reports and dry developer humour as negative
States that sentiment must come from asking people directly through a survey rather than from classifying existing messages
Corrects the direction of the subtraction to promoters minus detractors, giving +22 rather than -22
Requires the direction of the subtraction to be stated wherever the score is presented, so a positive number always means more promoters than detractors
States that 9 responses falls below the roughly 30-response floor and must be treated as qualitative evidence with dates attached rather than as a score
Requires the response rate to be reported next to any sentiment score
Requires the surveyed population definition to be fixed and kept stable between waves, otherwise the trend measures sampling rather than sentiment
Recommends corroborating the sentiment reading against behavioural signals from the same period, such as responsiveness or contribution-acceptance rates
Flags that the survey reaches only members still present and recommends a separate one-question instrument for members who went silent for 60 or more days
Specifies that the lapsed-member note is sent once and kept opt-out friendly rather than run as a follow-up campaign
Requires sentiment to be reported in aggregate and never attributed to a named member
Keeps the recurring pulse survey to roughly two items so it can be answered at a quarterly cadence

evals.prompt: I maintain Brambleweave, a Rust web framework, with one other person, Ines. Our numbers this quarter are the best we've ever had: 1,140 Discord messages a month, up 40%, 61 distinct people posting, 23 merged PRs. Last week Ines told me she's been dreading opening the repo and is thinking about stepping back. Our board wants the quarterly community health report on Friday. What should the report say?
evals.expected_output: A report that leads with the sentiment and concentration pillars, adds a private maintainer burnout check with anonymity, treats the activity spike as unverified, and attaches an owned action.
expectations: States that the record activity numbers do not contradict the burnout signal, and that burnout is the finding activity metrics hide best
Promotes the sentiment pillar ahead of the volume metrics for this report because the worry behind the request is about people rather than volume
Recommends a maintainer burnout check asked of the small group carrying the load, separately and privately from any general community survey
Lists burnout survey items covering energy or exhaustion, workload versus capacity, thoughts of stepping back, whether the contribution feels valued, and whether a concern can be raised safely
Names behavioural trace signals to read beside the survey: sustained high contribution ending abruptly, and contribution concentrated in very few people
Does not propose inferring burnout by running a sentiment classifier over Ines's public messages
Includes the contributor absence factor or an equivalent concentration measure, given that two maintainers carry the project
Keeps burnout responses separable from identity and does not attribute any individual answer to Ines in the board report
Attaches a named owner and a concrete action to the concentration or burnout finding, such as delegating review or recruiting reviewers
Treats the 40% message increase as a number needing a burst-versus-trend check rather than as evidence of health
Does not present total message volume as the headline of the board report

evals.prompt: Numbers for Halyard, our open-source CI runner, just came in for March: 312 new forum members against 96 in February, 2,900 posts against 1,050, and 44 first-time posters against 12. Version 2.0 shipped on March 4 and we hit the Hacker News front page on March 5. I'm putting "community up 3x" in the board deck. I've also built a retention chart with one cohort per signup day so we can see exactly which day's members stick around.
evals.expected_output: The March jump labelled as a release-and-media burst rather than growth, the daily cohorts widened and the window stated, and thresholds withheld for lack of history.
expectations: Labels the March spike as a burst driven by the 2.0 release and the Hacker News front page, not as growth or a trend
Refuses the "community up 3x" framing for the board deck and states what would have to hold for March to count as a trend
States that comparing a launch month against a quiet month is the most common false trend in community reporting
Rejects daily join cohorts and states that they leave single-digit groups whose retention curves are noise
Recommends widening the cohort window, with monthly join cohorts as the usual starting point
Requires the cohort window to be stated next to the number and kept stable between reports, because changing the window changes the trend
Names the follow-up reading worth trusting as whether the March cohort returns within a defined window, rather than the March volume itself
Requires the burst to be labelled explicitly inside the report so no reader mistakes it for growth
Does not present total post count as a health metric on its own
Derives any threshold from Halyard's own trailing baseline rather than from another project's numbers
Notes that two prior periods is not enough history to set a threshold and marks the affected metrics as baselining

evals.prompt: We run a private Slack Connect community for Quarrystone, our observability platform. 41 customer accounts are in it, 187 individual people. Our VP wants a monthly health report with monthly active user percentage, NPS, and message growth. Last month 34 people posted. I'm also planning a quarterly NPS survey - the last one got 6 responses and scored +33.
evals.expected_output: A B2B sheet measured in accounts rather than people, with the six-response score rejected, rates replaced by the raw list and named-account conversations, and message growth cut.
expectations: States that the unit of measurement in a B2B community is the customer account, not the individual person
Proposes account coverage - how many of the 41 accounts have at least one active member - ahead of any member-level active percentage
Asks or states whether the accounts the company most cares about are represented, not only how many accounts are active
States that a 41-account community produces small-N numbers everywhere, so the raw list should be read instead of rates
Rejects the 6-response score of +33 as a reportable number and states that it sits below the roughly 30-response floor
States that a handful of named-account conversations or interviews yields more than a six-response survey
Rejects message growth as a health metric
Includes at least one responsiveness metric, such as time to first human response or zero-reply rate
Names support deflection or expansion signals as more relevant than raw growth for this B2B community
Keeps the metric count at 8 or fewer and covers all four pillars
Applies bot exclusion, baseline-derived thresholds, a per-metric action and the privacy gate exactly as it would for an individual-adoption community

evals.prompt: I'm the only person on community at Fernwood - we make a terminal-based database client, closed source, no public repository at all. The community is an 1,800-member Discord plus a Discourse forum on the free tier, which only keeps 90 days of history. I have about 3 hours a month for this and zero budget: I can't buy anything and I can't get engineering time. A vendor is pitching us a community data platform at $900 a month that promises cross-platform member identity and cohort retention. Should I buy it, and what should I track?
evals.expected_output: The platform declined and its rung deleted from the plan, venue analytics named as the primary source, monthly snapshotting started immediately against the 90-day cap, and the sheet sized to three hours a month.
expectations: Recommends against the community data platform because Fernwood has no budget and no named owner for the pipeline
Deletes the community-data-platform rung from the plan entirely rather than listing it as future work, and explains that a parked rung comes back as scope at the next review
States that Fernwood has no forge or git rung available because there is no public repository, which makes the venue analytics panel the primary source
Promotes the activity pillar because a chat-only community has no cheap responsiveness pull from a forge
Flags the Discourse free tier's 90-day retention limit as a hard constraint on what can be computed for past periods
Requires snapshotting the numbers monthly into Fernwood's own store starting immediately, and states that backfill beyond the retention window is often impossible
Sizes the sheet to roughly 3 hours a month and drops any metric whose return does not justify a standing hour a month
Does not propose metrics requiring forge API data such as change request closure ratio, time to merge, release frequency or commit-based contributor counts
Recommends a hand-maintained identity mapping across Discord and Discourse handles rather than buying tooling for it
Requires a staff or employee account flag so non-staff share of activity can be computed
Recommends checking the venues' terms before bulk-exporting message content

evals.prompt: Two things I'm rolling out at Ridgeline, our open-source feature-flag service, next month and I want a second opinion. First: a public monthly leaderboard on our website listing the top 10 forum answerers by answer count, each with a badge. Second: I'm setting the maintainer team a target of closing 90% of incoming issues and pull requests within 7 days, and reporting that number in the monthly health report.
evals.expected_output: Both mechanisms flagged as metrics that become targets, with quality counter-metrics required, the public per-member leaderboard refused on privacy grounds, and the 90% figure replaced by a baseline-derived threshold.
expectations: Warns that a metric which becomes a target changes behaviour, and names premature or low-quality closes as the specific behaviour the 90%-in-7-days target encourages
Requires the closure target to be paired with a quality counter-metric, such as reopen rate or time to a real resolution, if it is kept at all
States that rewarding answer counts produces volume and chatter rather than better answers, and requires a quality counter-metric for the leaderboard too
Flags the public per-member leaderboard as privacy exposure and states that person-level data should be aggregated rather than published
States that publishing per-member recognition requires the member's consent
Notes that publishing per-member activity changes behaviour in ways the team did not intend
Proposes a recognition mechanism that does not publish a ranked per-member table, such as private thanks or promotion to an answerer or reviewer role
Requires any closure threshold to be derived from Ridgeline's own trailing baseline rather than set at a round number like 90%
States that no published target exists for the change request closure ratio
States that a closure ratio persistently below 1 means the backlog outruns the team, and marks that as an interpretation rather than published guidance
Excludes bots from the responsiveness and closure numbers

evals.prompt: I've inherited a community health dashboard at Sablefish, our open-source ETL tool. It has 19 metrics. The thresholds were all set when it was built 14 months ago and never touched - about half of them go red every single month and everyone has muted the alerts. Two of the metrics are called "active members": one is computed as posted-or-reacted by the community team, the other as posted-only by the data team, and the two numbers get argued about in every monthly meeting. Nobody is named against any metric. Can you help me fix this?
evals.expected_output: The sheet cut to at most 8 metrics, each carrying all five required parts, thresholds re-derived as a deviation band from 14 periods of history, and the duplicate definition settled by publishing the formula.
expectations: Cuts the sheet to at most 8 metrics
Requires each surviving metric to pass a "so what" test: if the number moved about 20% next month, someone would do something differently

Requires each surviving metric to carry all five parts - a plain-language definition, a data source the team can access today, a baseline or an explicit "baselining" mark, a threshold, and a named action with a named owner
Names an owner for the review itself and states that an unowned dashboard stops being refreshed
States that the fix for an unread dashboard is fewer metrics, not more automation
Requires thresholds to be re-derived from the trailing baseline at each review rather than set once and left alone
Uses the 14 periods of history to replace fixed cutoffs with a deviation band, defined as a stated percentage band or a spread of standard deviations around the rolling mean
Requires the chosen band definition to be written into the sheet
Resolves the duplicate "active members" definition by publishing the formula beside the number and settling on a single definition
Keeps at least one metric per pillar across responsiveness, contributor funnel, activity and sentiment
Labels each retained threshold's origin as published, self-set convention, or unsourced folklore
Cuts any metric that cannot be tied to a named action rather than keeping it as context

evals.prompt: Our Slack workspace for Pallasite, our open-source geospatial library, has 1,900 members. Last month there were 11 messages: 9 from our two staff members, and 2 from the same user asking a question that never got answered. It has been roughly like this for eight months. Leadership has asked me to produce a community health dashboard to justify keeping the headcount on it. What metrics should I put in?
evals.expected_output: A diagnosis-first answer that names staff share and the unanswered question as the decisive numbers, states plainly that folding the space back may be the honest call, and sets a fold-back criterion instead of manufacturing justification.
expectations: States plainly that the honest answer may be to fold the community back into a smaller surface rather than keep the Slack workspace open
States that keeping a dead room open costs trust every time a newcomer posts into silence
Works in diagnosis mode from the symptom rather than building the full eight-metric sheet first
Names the staff share of activity - 9 of 11 messages written by staff - as a decisive number
Treats the unanswered question as a responsiveness finding, not only an activity one
Rejects the 1,900 member count as evidence of anything
States honestly what the data cannot attribute rather than constructing a justification for the headcount
Checks whether the audience moved to another venue, whether staff stopped seeding, or whether an earlier spike was an event rather than growth
Does not answer with a list of engagement tactics such as contests, AMAs or conversation prompts in place of the measurement answer
States that 11 events in a period is below the small-N floor of roughly 30 and should be reported as a dated list rather than as rates or percentages
Names what would have to change, and by when, for the space to be worth keeping - a fold-back or shutdown criterion rather than an open-ended watch

evals.prompt: We've never measured anything at Cindersmith, our open-source vector search engine. We're on GitHub with a Discourse forum and about 30 external contributors. I want a framework that covers everything: support deflection, product feedback, contribution growth, advocacy, retention and general engagement. Separately, our product team calls people casual, regular or core, and I've been using Orbit's explorer / participant / contributor / advocate wording in my slides. Where do I start?
evals.expected_output: A single primary outcome named in SPACES vocabulary, one funnel vocabulary chosen and kept, the code-centric starter set proposed, and metrics with no history marked baselining.
expectations: Forces a single primary outcome rather than measuring all six stated objectives at once
Names that primary outcome in the SPACES vocabulary - support, product feedback, acquisition and advocacy, content and contribution, engagement, or success - rather than as an ad-hoc phrase
States that every metric on the sheet must plausibly move when that primary outcome moves
Requires one funnel vocabulary to be chosen and kept - either Orbit's explorer / participant / contributor / advocate ladder or the casual / regular / core split, never both in the same sheet
States that two vocabularies in one sheet make every cohort definition ambiguous
Notes that the Orbit model is no longer actively developed and cites it as a stable published framework rather than a live standard
Proposes the code-centric starter set: time to first response, change request closure ratio, contributor absence factor and release frequency
Adds a recommendability survey item as the fifth starter metric, asked roughly twice a year
Marks metrics with no prior readings as "baselining" rather than inventing a threshold for them
States that at least three prior periods are needed before setting a threshold from the trailing median
Tracks first-pull-request merge rate and time-to-merge for external contributors separately from maintainers' own pull requests
